Haroun Bouazzi : la création de l’Autre: Haroun Bouazzi: The Creation of the Other Behind the Controversy
La Converse a interrogé des sociologues: La Converse spoke with sociologists to unpack the sentence that changed everything, in particular the “creation of the Other.”
Quand on a vu passer les dizaines d’arti: When we saw dozens of articles on Haroun Bouazzi go by over the past two weeks, we wondered how La Converse could weigh in without adding fuel to a fire that was already burning bright enough. In the end, while listening to the Québec solidaire MNA’s speech and then his interview on Radio-Canada’s morning show, our attention was caught by a concept that kept coming up: the creation of the Other.
Si le débat s’est cristallisé autour de: While the debate crystallized around the question of whether or not Haroun Bouazzi said that the National Assembly was racist, we chose instead to focus on this concept, which is used in sociology, among other fields, in order to analyze this political episode.
Nous ne cherchons ni à l’accuser ni à le: We are not trying to accuse him or defend him, but to shed scientific light on this affair.
<strong>Les dernières semaines ont été m: The past few weeks have been turbulent at the National Assembly. Who is racist? Who isn’t? Who feels insulted? Who should apologize? These are all debates that have filled newspaper pages and fuelled television and radio programs. At the centre of this storm, MNA Haroun Bouazzi stands accused of insinuating that his colleagues are racist. A closer look.

Ces citations sont extraites de l’émissi: These quotes are taken from the program Tout un matin, broadcast on Radio-Canada on November 15. Journalist Patrick Masbourian was hosting Haroun Bouazzi, the Québec solidaire MNA for Maurice-Richard, after remarks he made at a gala set off a large-scale media and political controversy.
Au fil des jours, les chroniques négativ: As the days went by, negative columns piled up in the newspapers. Some called him “ungrateful” or a “bridge burner.” Disavowed by his own party, Québec solidaire, he received only a few rare official messages of support. Not to mention social media, where a wave of harassment crashed down: “He should resign,” “This guy is insulting us,” “An Islamist at work,” “He’s a piece of crap”…
Pris dans la tempête, Haroun Bouazzi a a: Caught in the storm, Haroun Bouazzi announced last Wednesday that he would be absent from the Blue Room for a few days. At the time of writing, the MNA for Maurice-Richard had not responded to our interview request.
Afin de comprendre ce qui a déclenché un: To understand what set off such a public pillorying, La Converse spoke with sociologists to unpack the sentence that changed everything, and more specifically the concept of the “creation of the Other.” To do that, we first need to go back a few weeks.
<strong>Un gala pour célébrer l’excellen: A gala celebrating excellence in the Maghrebi community
Au cours de la soirée du samedi 2 novemb: On the evening of Saturday, November 2, a room full of guests attended the traditional Gala d’Excellence of the <l1>Fondation Club Avenir</l1>. For 22 years, the foundation has been celebrating members of Quebec’s Maghrebi community. “Every year, we organize this event in a festive atmosphere and invite business people, artists, diplomatic representatives, parliamentarians, at both the federal and provincial levels,” explains Bachir Halimi, one of the organization’s founders. “Essentially, it lets us showcase the positive achievements of our community, which chose Quebec as its host society.”
Après avoir admiré une exposition artist: After admiring an art exhibit over cocktails, guests attended the awards ceremony in the Amphithéâtre Banque Nationale at HEC Montréal. In the room, faces were smiling, and the speeches that punctuated the ceremony were warmly applauded. Elite athletes, artists, entrepreneurs, lawyers and students: the year’s 10 winners came up one after another. Already invited to present an award the previous year, MNA Haroun Bouazzi took the stage again at this 22<sup>nd</sup> edition of the gala.
« C’est d’autant plus important aujourd’: “It’s all the more important today – and God knows I see it at the National Assembly every day – the construction of this Other who is Maghrebi, Muslim, who is Black, who is Indigenous, and of their culture which, by definition, would be dangerous or inferior.” – Haroun Bouazzi, Québec solidaire MNA for Maurice-Richard
Costume bleu nuit, cravate rouge carmin: In a midnight-blue suit, a crimson tie and sneakers, the Québec solidaire MNA looked at ease. Mr. Bouazzi devoted his remarks to “one of the reasons” he went into politics: the issue of racism.
« Il n’y a pas de races humaines, évidem: “There are no human races, obviously; there are races that are constructed by society, which creates a category to which it assigns a culture that, by definition, is dangerous, that is inferior. And after 22 years, what you do is very important for breaking down the construction of these mechanisms of racism,” said the elected official, unaware that his next sentence would set off an enormous media and political controversy. “It’s all the more important today – and God knows I see it at the National Assembly every day – the construction of this Other who is Maghrebi, Muslim, who is Black, who is Indigenous, and of their culture which, by definition, would be dangerous or inferior.”
Au total, ce discours aura duré moins de: In all, the speech lasted less than five minutes. Applauded by the audience, he returned to his seat, and the evening went on. “I can’t speak for everyone who was there, but it seems to me that, in the moment, what people understood was that he said there is racism at the National Assembly. And that’s nothing new, I mean, everyone knows racism exists everywhere. I don’t think anyone can tell me there isn’t any, but racism is expressed to different degrees, and that doesn’t mean the MNAs are racists,” says Bachir Halimi, co-founder of the Fondation Club Avenir, which organized the gala.

Halimi souligne que des représentants: Mr. Halimi points out that representatives of several political parties are invited every year, and he explains that before they go on stage, a note is handed out to the guests of honour. “We ask them to avoid politics, because we’re a non-partisan organization. That said, as soon as you talk about integration or social success in a host society, it’s necessarily political. Mr. Bouazzi chose to talk about something that’s close to his heart, I think,” Mr. Halimi reflects. He would have preferred that the media talk about the Fondation Club Avenir for its work.
La soirée se poursuit donc dans les rire: The evening thus carried on with laughter, with a performance by comedian Oussama Fares, and finally with music from DJ Zales. It was only much later that the little tune of scandal began to be heard.
Comble de l’ironie, c’est Haroun Bouazzi: In a twist of irony, it was Haroun Bouazzi himself who posted <l1>the video of his speech</l1> online on November 5, on Facebook and YouTube. While it attracted relatively little attention at first, with only a few hundred views, it drew renewed interest once journalists reported on it. Soon, all anyone talked about was “the Bouazzi affair.”
Chroniqueurs et politiciens accusent le: Columnists and politicians accused the MNA of calling the National Assembly, and by extension its members, racist. Unsurprisingly, Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon lambasted Haroun Bouazzi’s “wokeism,” equating his remarks with “intimidation.”
Du côté des libéraux, la députée <l1>Mar: On the Liberal side, MNA <l1>Marwah Rizqy</l1> said no one had ever made her feel “dangerous or inferior” at the National Assembly, noting that she is of Moroccan origin. At the same time, Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois and Ruba Ghazal, the two spokespersons of his own party, Québec solidaire, called the MNA for Maurice-Richard to order.
« Je n’ai jamais dit que l’Assemblée nat: “I never said that the National Assembly was racist.” – Haroun Bouazzi, MNA for Maurice-Richard
Le vendredi 15 novembre, M. Bouazzi est: On Friday, November 15, Mr. Bouazzi was interviewed by <l1>Patrick Masbourian</l1> on Radio-Canada’s morning show. Pressed by the journalist to apologize, he reiterated his position. “I never said that the National Assembly was racist,” said the MNA, who believes his words were “distorted” and “interpreted” the wrong way. “As a Quebecer, I have a responsibility to bear witness and to fight for my principles, out of love for Quebec and out of love for my people. It takes courage, and it’s true that there’s a headwind,” he added.
Une entrevue qui demeure à ce jour son u: That interview remains, to this day, his only media appearance on the subject. During the conversation, he tried to clarify his thinking, in particular the concept of the “creation of the Other,” which is at the heart of the sentence he is accused of having uttered.
Après plusieurs jours de bras de fer au: After several days of a tug-of-war within Québec solidaire, the party adopted <l1>a motion</l1> denouncing “the unjustified instrumentalization regularly suffered by immigrants,” while affirming “clearly and unambiguously that Québec solidaire does not support and has never maintained that the National Assembly and its members are racist.” Haroun Bouazzi himself backed the resolution on November 17.
Deux jours plus tard, c’est <l1>sur le r: Two days later, the MNA decided to explain himself publicly <l1>on the social network X</l1>, walking a tightrope. While he did not offer the formal apology demanded by some, Haroun Bouazzi clarified his position: “On what promises to be a difficult day for Québec solidaire’s parliamentary wing, I want to take the time to say some important things. First of all, I reaffirm my commitment to working alongside my colleagues in the Québec solidaire caucus, in the service of our movement and the causes it defends to improve people’s lives. In that spirit, I join them in saying that I do not consider the National Assembly and its members to be racist and that this is not the party’s position.”
Mercredi dernier, celui qui n’en est pas: Last Wednesday, the man, who is no stranger to controversy, decided to take “a few days” of rest with his family. Columnist and former Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Amir Khadir is one of the few political figures to come to his defence. He denounced a “public lynching” and an “orchestrated political execution.”
<strong>La création de l’Autre : un phén: The creation of the Other: a phenomenon rooted in history
« Ce qu’il se passe, avec l’affaire Boua: “What’s happening with the Bouazzi affair is an extreme media reaction to a speech that is, in the end, completely ordinary,” says Catherine Larochelle, a history professor specializing in questions of otherness and postcolonialism. In her view, the affair has put the spotlight on something that is far from new, since the creation of the Other is a phenomenon rooted in history and studied since the 1960s.
« L’altérisation s’appuie sur des représ: “Othering relies on cultural representations that have existed for centuries,” she says. “Yet there isn’t necessarily any intent [to create the Other]. It’s both a lack of knowledge and the cultural legacy of unconscious biases that lead some people to make statements or pass laws that contribute to this creation of the Other.”
Il s’agirait d’un processus insidieux de: It is an insidious process of stigmatizing the Other, that is, anyone who is different. “And since immigration is often associated with racialized populations, that creates an equation in which there are Quebecers, who are mostly white, and then everyone else.”
Au-delà de l’indignation que suscite l’a: Beyond the outrage the Bouazzi affair has generated, the debate reflects deeper social dynamics and phenomena, including the denial of racism, according to the expert. “The substance of Haroun Bouazzi’s thinking was never discussed in the debate. People didn’t want to discuss the construction of the Other.” A reaction from the political sphere that doesn’t surprise Catherine Larochelle.
D’après ses observations, les personnes: From her observations, racialized people are often seen as less entitled to speak about racism in Quebec. “I see it clearly when I give talks on the subject: I get a favourable reception, unlike a racialized person who would say the exact same things,” she says flatly.
<strong>Ignorance et fragilité blanche :: Ignorance and white fragility: structural drivers for stifling debate
Selon Leila Benhadjoudja, professeure de: According to Leila Benhadjoudja, a sociology professor at the University of Ottawa, “[denying] this ‘construction of the Other,’ as Mr. Bouazzi put it, is wanting to silence those who speak out and maintain a power relationship.” This strategy of repression, known as silencing, aims to prevent critical voices, particularly those of racialized communities, from fully expressing themselves in the public or institutional sphere.
« Ce qu’on observe souvent, c’est une in: “What we often see is a reversal of roles: those who denounce racism end up marginalized, sometimes even seen as aggressors.” – Leila Benhadjoudja, sociology professor at the University of Ottawa
Selon elle, cette dynamique se manifeste: In her view, this dynamic is especially apparent in institutions of power like the National Assembly. “What we often see is a reversal of roles: those who denounce racism end up marginalized, sometimes even seen as aggressors. In the ‘Bouazzi affair,’” she says, making air quotes with her fingers, “this took the form of an attempt to portray the white majority as the victim, simply because racism was mentioned.”
M<sup>me</sup> Benhadjoudja associe cett: Ms. Benhadjoudja links this creation of the Other to two key concepts: white ignorance, theorized by Charles Mills, and white fragility, formulated by Robin DiAngelo. “White ignorance,” she explains, “is an active production of denial.” “It’s not that we don’t know, but rather that we choose to ignore,” she insists. “This denial makes it possible, among other things, to maintain a façade of innocence while perpetuating domination.”
La fragilité blanche, elle, désigne les: White fragility, meanwhile, refers to the defensive reactions of white individuals when faced with discussions about racism or their privilege. “When racism comes up, the white majority gets indignant and says it’s hurt. This dynamic then forces racialized communities to apologize for having denounced racism. It’s yet another strategy aimed at maintaining silence, at stifling critical voices,” she says.
Pour M<sup>me</sup> Benhadjoudja, ce <em: For Ms. Benhadjoudja, this silencing is part of a broader myth: that of a post-racial society. This idea, that Western societies have overcome racial inequalities, serves to divert attention from the systemic structures that perpetuate those inequalities. “We want to believe we’ve achieved perfect equality: social, racial and gender justice. Yet all you have to do is listen to racialized communities or look at the social and scientific data to see that racism persists,” she says.
Ce mythe, loin d’être anodin, joue un rô: Far from harmless, this myth plays an active role in maintaining power relations. This logic, rooted in a neoliberal framework, places responsibility on individuals and thereby prevents any questioning of institutions. “By reducing racism to individual behaviours, we depoliticize the issue and divert attention from the systemic structures responsible for racial inequalities,” she explains.
M<sup>me</sup> Benhadjoudja souligne que: M<sup>s</sup>. Benhadjoudja points out that, while biological racism has lost legitimacy, it has evolved into a cultural form. “Today, people talk about integration challenges or cultural differences, but the substance remains the same: presenting the Other as a problem.” Citing African American sociologist W. E. B. Du Bois, she asks: “What does it feel like to be seen as a problem? Who is singled out as a problem in political or media discourse? Which communities are considered threats? Who holds the power to define the Other, to construct this otherness? Who sits in decision-making bodies?” she lists.
Cette inversion des responsabilités sera: This reversal of responsibility is particularly problematic, she argues. “What becomes a source of outrage isn’t that racism exists, but that someone dares to talk about it!” she exclaims. “Refusing to see the racist nature of these discourses is the height of absurdity!”
À Montréal, la jeunesse racisée témoigne: In Montréal, racialized youth describe a feeling of “stigmatization” in public debate.
<strong>« Les jeunes ont l’impression qu: “Young people feel like their culture is being demonized”
Pétillante et directe, Marie-Christine J: Bubbly and direct, Marie-Christine Jeanty uses humour to tackle complex subjects. She works for the City of Montréal, but prefers to introduce herself as the former vice-president of the Conseil interculturel de Montréal, a role that better reflects her path in the fight against inequality. It is a commitment passed down by her Haitian parents, themselves very active in the fight against racism and other social causes. Her mother, Maryse Alcindor, became the first Black woman to serve as deputy minister of Immigration and Cultural Communities, in 2005. Her father, who died four years ago, was chair of the board of directors of the Maison d’Haïti in Montréal.
Pour M<sup>me</sup> Jeanty, qui vit dans: For M<sup>s</sup>. Jeanty, who lives in Mr. Bouazzi’s riding, he has nothing to be blamed for. “What he said are things I hear and see. Young immigrants, for example, often think they don’t belong here,” she says, even though she isn’t surprised by the scale the controversy has taken on.
Selon elle, la quête identitaire des jeu: In her view, the identity struggles of the young people she works with can be attributed to negative discourse about immigrant, racialized and marginalized communities. This “construction of the Other” would therefore have repercussions on those who are its target. “Young people often tell me they feel like their culture is being demonized. They can’t be fully themselves in this society. So they ask themselves: ‘What is our place?’ They feel like they never do enough to prove they’re ‘good immigrants,’” she reports. “‘We’re always made to feel like we’re the Other, all the time,’” they confide to Marie-Christine Jeanty.
C’est en effet le sentiment qu’Aya, une: That is indeed the feeling Aya, a young international relations student, says she had about the controversy surrounding Haroun Bouazzi. “Stories like Mr. Bouazzi’s show that we don’t really have freedom of expression, and it discourages us enormously when it comes to politics. No matter what we say, no matter what we think, even if we try to say it properly and in a well-meaning way, it’s going to be misinterpreted. I find that disheartening and discouraging for young people,” she laments.
La jeune femme y voit « un double standa: The young woman sees “a double standard” and outrage that seems to depend on who is speaking. “Mr. Legault, our premier, sometimes says very disparaging things about immigrants. For example, when he said that <l1>100% of the housing crisis is due to immigrants</l1>, I didn’t understand why it didn’t provoke more reaction,” Aya points out.
Imen, 22 ans et membre du forum jeunesse: Imen, 22, a member of the Saint-Michel youth forum, also takes a sceptical view of the political world. Still, she prefers to hold on to hope: “Honestly, having people like him in politics gives me back some confidence. Despite everything he’s been through, I focus on the fact that there are people like him to move things forward and to serve citizens.”
